lines.text: Tonight, the Moon starts coming closer. And it never stops.

sentences.text: Tonight, the Moon starts coming closer.

lines.text: Right now it's about three hundred eighty-four thousand kilometers away, drifting off three point eight centimeters a year. Tonight, it reverses. A thought experiment, built from real physics.

lines.text: Watch the number. It only goes down.
Two hundred eighty-eight thousand. A third wider. And the sea already feels it: more than twice the tidal pull.

sentences.text: And the sea already feels it: more than twice the tidal pull.

lines.text: Halve the distance, and the water starts to climb.

sentences.text: Halve the distance, and the water starts to climb.

lines.text: Half the distance. Twice as wide. Eight times the tidal pull.
Not a measured height. Just the idea: the whole ocean, lifted from above.

sentences.text: Just the idea: the whole ocean, lifted from above.

lines.text: And the night is about to change.

sentences.text: And the night is about to change.

lines.text: One hundred fifty thousand. Six and a half times the moonlight. Your shadow is sharp on the sand.

lines.text: And it's faster. One lap takes about seven days, not twenty-seven.

lines.text: It's bigger than the Sun now. So what happens when they line up?

lines.text: One hundred thousand. Nearly four times wider. Its shadow on Earth is wider, and eclipses come far more often. Not every month, because the orbit is tilted. But often.

lines.text: Closer. Faster. And the ground feels it too.

sentences.text: And the ground feels it too.

lines.text: Seventy thousand. More than a hundred sixty times today's tidal pull. The solid ground already rises and falls tens of centimeters a day. Here, it would flex far more.

lines.text: Soon, the Moon rises on the wrong side of the sky.

lines.text: Fifty thousand. Nearly eight times wider. One lap takes about a day and a quarter, close to how fast the Earth turns.

lines.text: Forty-two thousand. It hangs still.
Then it slides the wrong way. It rises in the west.

lines.text: Thirty thousand. Twenty-five. Twenty.

Around eighteen thousand kilometers is the Roche limit: where Earth's tides pull harder than the Moon's own gravity holds it together. That's if the Moon acts like a fluid. A perfectly rigid Moon could come to about nine and a half thousand.

lines.text: At eighteen thousand, it's more than twenty times wider than tonight. A wall of grey, straining.

lines.text: And then it does something no Moon should survive.

lines.text: It comes apart. Not an explosion. A stretch.
The rock spreads along its old orbit, and over time it can flatten into a ring.

lines.text: No Moon. Just a bright band, horizon to horizon.
